q.intro.text: Sam’s arcade card: the receipts say four games cost thirteen dollars in total, card included, and ten games cost twenty-eight dollars. Sam has forty dollars to spend, card included. How many games can Sam play? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps: name the quantities, find the rate, walk back to the start, then let the story decide the answer.

e.step0.text: Two quantities change together. The input g is the number of games played: a count, and g equals zero means the card is new. The output C is the total cost in dollars, card included.

e.step1.text: From the first receipt to the second: six more games, fifteen dollars more. The rate is fifteen divided by six, two dollars and fifty cents per game. Dollars per game: output unit per input unit.

e.step2.text: Thirteen dollars is not the start: it is after four games. Walk back four games: thirteen minus two and a half times four is three dollars, the card itself. So C equals two point five g, plus three. Units check: dollars per game times games is dollars, plus dollars. And games come whole: the model is dots, not a solid line.

e.step3.text: Forty dollars to spend is a limit: two point five g, plus three, is at most forty, so g is at most fourteen point eight. Not fourteen point eight games, and not fifteen: fifteen games cost forty dollars and fifty cents. The story decides the direction: fourteen games, for thirty-eight dollars.

e.why.text: Quick check: why fourteen games, when fourteen point eight is closer to fifteen?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. The limit decides: check the neighbor. Fifteen games break the forty dollars, fourteen games fit. Nearest is not the rule.

e.why.near.text: Rounding to the nearest gives fifteen, and fifteen games cost forty dollars and fifty cents: Sam cannot pay that. The direction comes from the limit.

e.why.drop.text: Here dropping the decimal lands on fourteen, but only by luck. If Sam needed at least forty dollars worth, dropping would leave him short. The reason is the limit.

t.intro.text: Your turn. A team runs a car wash. After ten cars their profit is negative eighty dollars, still in the hole. After twenty-five cars it is forty dollars. The rate is done for you: one hundred twenty divided by fifteen, eight dollars per car.

t.b.text: Walk back to w equals zero. What is the profit before any car?

t.b.ok.text: Yes: negative eighty, minus eight times ten, is negative one hundred sixty. The team spent one hundred sixty dollars on supplies before the first car. P equals eight w, minus one hundred sixty.

t.b.first.text: Negative eighty is the profit after ten cars, not at the start. Walk back ten cars, at eight dollars each.

t.b.sign.text: Walking back undoes the earnings: take eight times ten away, do not add it.

t.b.no.text: Start from ten cars and negative eighty dollars, and go back ten cars: negative eighty, minus eight times ten.

t.ineq.text: The team wants a profit of at least two hundred fifty dollars. Which inequality says that?

t.ineq.ok.text: Yes: at least means two hundred fifty dollars or more, two hundred fifty included.

t.ineq.strict.text: At least two hundred fifty includes two hundred fifty itself: use greater than or equal, not greater than.

t.ineq.rev.text: At least means two hundred fifty or more. Less than or equal would mean two hundred fifty or less.

t.ineq.eq.text: A goal of at least allows many profits, not exactly one: use an inequality.

t.w.text: Eight w minus one hundred sixty, at least two hundred fifty, gives w at least fifty-one point two five. How many cars must they wash?

t.w.ok.text: Yes: fifty-two cars. Fifty-one cars give two hundred forty-eight dollars, just short. Fifty-two give two hundred fifty-six. Enough rounds up.

t.w.near.text: Fifty-one point two five rounds to fifty-one, but fifty-one cars give only two hundred forty-eight dollars: short. Enough goes up.

t.w.frac.text: Nobody washes a quarter of a car: w is a count. Pick the whole number that reaches the goal.

t.w.no.text: w must be at least fifty-one point two five, and a whole number: the first whole number past it.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked fourteen, and you were right. Now you know why: the model gives fourteen point eight, and the limit rounds down.

q.cb.near.text: At the start you picked fifteen: the nearest whole number to fourteen point eight. But fifteen games cost forty dollars and fifty cents. A limit sets the direction.

q.cb.prop.text: At the start you picked twelve: that treats thirteen dollars for four games as three twenty-five per game. The card is paid once. Each game is two fifty.

q.cb.none.text: Rate from two data points, walk back to the start, and let the story decide which whole number counts.

p.intro.text: A print shop charges twelve dollars setup plus seventy-five cents per poster. Ava has exactly fifty dollars to spend and says: fifty minus twelve, divided by point seven five, is fifty point six seven, so fifty-one posters cost exactly fifty dollars. Is Ava right?

p.test.text: Let’s test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. Put fifty-one back into the model: fifty dollars and twenty-five cents. Ava’s rounding changed the total.

p.c2.text: Right. The dots jump from forty-nine fifty to fifty twenty-five: the fifty-dollar line passes between them and hits no dot.

p.c3.text: Right. The exact question has no answer. The question with a limit does: fifty posters.

p.no.round.text: Rounding changes the input, so it changes the total: fifty-one posters cost fifty dollars and twenty-five cents. Exactly means exactly.

p.no.eq.text: The equation has a solution, fifty point six seven, but posters are counted: the story only allows whole numbers.

p.no.drop.text: Fifty posters cost forty-nine fifty, not fifty. Dropping the decimal does not make it exact either.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That’s a proof: an exact target on a count can have no solution, and rounding does not create one. A limit, at most or at least, always has a whole number answer in the right direction.
